claim: Different drugs stabilize distinct active states of their G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) targets, allowing coupling to different effectors.
source: The prevailing model for the variety in drug responses is that different drugs stabilize distinct active states of their G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) targets, allowing coupling to different effectors.
evidence: This is stated as the prevailing model in the field, representing established scientific understanding.

claim: Golgi and surface pools of DOR both inhibit cAMP in rat neuroendocrine cells.
source: We have shown that Golgi and surface pools of DOR both inhibit cAMP, but engage distinct conformational biosensors in response to the same ligand in rat neuroendocrine cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Golgi and surface pools of DOR engage distinct conformational biosensors in response to the same ligand in rat neuroendocrine cells.
source: We have shown that Golgi and surface pools of DOR both inhibit cAMP, but engage distinct conformational biosensors in response to the same ligand in rat neuroendocrine cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: DOR recruits arrestins on the surface but not on the Golgi.
source: Further, DOR recruits arrestins on the surface but not on the Golgi.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The local environment determines the active states of receptors for any given drug, allowing GPCRs to couple to different effectors at different subcellular locations.
source: Our results suggest that the local environment determines the active states of receptors for any given drug, allowing GPCRs to couple to different effectors at different subcellular locations.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, inferred from the experimental results presented.

claim: Binding to both agonist and G protein stabilizes an active state of the receptor, among a number of states that a given receptor may sample.
source: Recent studies support an allosteric model of coupling in which binding to both agonist and G protein stabilizes an active state of the receptor, among a number of states that a given receptor may sample (Okude et al., 2015; Weis and Kobilka, 2018; Nygaard et al., 2013; Ye et al., 2016; Manglik et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: β-arrestins interact with GPCRs through additional receptor conformations and can serve as scaffolds for kinase signaling pathways.
source: In addition to canonical G protein effectors, β-arrestins interact with GPCRs through additional receptor conformations and can serve as scaffolds for kinase signaling pathways (Gurevich and Gurevich, 2019a; Liu et al., 2012; Wingler et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Efforts to develop compounds that stabilize one set of conformations and therefore bias the receptor response to specific pathways have been promising but difficult to translate to in vivo models.
source: However, efforts to develop compounds that stabilize one set of conformations and therefore bias the receptor response to specific pathways have been promising but difficult to translate to in vivo models (Gillis et al., 2020; Luttrell et al., 2015; Viscusi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DOR localizes primarily to the Golgi in neuronal cells, with a small amount on the plasma membrane.
source: DOR localizes primarily to the Golgi in neuronal cells, with a small amount on the plasma membrane (PM) (Kim and von Zastrow, 2003; Shiwarski et al., 2017a; Zhang et al., 1998; Cahill et al., 2001a; Wang and Pickel, 2001; Mittal et al., 2013; Shiwarski et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DOR can be activated both on the PM and the Golgi by synthetic agonists.
source: DOR can be activated both on the PM and the Golgi by synthetic agonists, but whether the two activation states are different is not clear (Stoeber et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Relocating DOR from intracellular compartments to the PM increases the ability of DOR agonists to relieve pain.
source: Relocating DOR from intracellular compartments to the PM increases the ability of DOR agonists to relieve pain (Shiwarski et al., 2017a; Mittal et al., 2013; Cahill et al., 2001b; Patwardhan et al., 2005), illustrating the importance of understanding whether DOR activation on the Golgi is different from that on the PM.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DOR on the PM, when activated by SNC80, can recruit both a nanobody-based sensor and a G protein-based sensor that read out active DOR conformations, as well as β-arrestins.
source: We have shown that DOR on the PM, when activated by the selective DOR agonist SNC80, can recruit both a nanobody-based sensor and a G protein-based sensor that read out active DOR conformations, as well as β-arrestins.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: DOR in the Golgi apparatus, when activated by SNC80, recruits the nanobody sensor, but not the G protein-based sensor or β-arrestins.
source: In contrast, DOR in the Golgi apparatus, when activated by the same ligand, recruits the nanobody sensor, but not the G protein-based sensor or β-arrestins.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Golgi-localized DOR is competent to inhibit cAMP.
source: Nevertheless, Golgi-localized DOR is competent to inhibit cAMP.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nanobody and miniG protein biosensors differentially engage the μ-opioid receptor (MOR) and the κ-opioid receptor (KOR) activated by different agonists in vitro.
source: These sensors differentially engage the μ-opioid receptor (MOR) and the κ-opioid receptor (KOR) activated by different agonists in vitro (Livingston et al., 2018) or in the PM (Stoeber et al., 2020), suggesting that they can provide a readout of conformational heterogeneity in agonist-stabilized active states.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nanobody and miniG protein biosensors differentially engage the μ-opioid receptor (MOR) and the κ-opioid receptor (KOR) activated by different agonists in the PM.
source: These sensors differentially engage the μ-opioid receptor (MOR) and the κ-opioid receptor (KOR) activated by different agonists in vitro (Livingston et al., 2018) or in the PM (Stoeber et al., 2020), suggesting that they can provide a readout of conformational heterogeneity in agonist-stabilized active states.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DOR is highly similar to MOR and KOR in the intracellular regions recognized by the sensors.
source: Because DOR is highly similar to MOR and KOR in the intracellular regions recognized by the sensors (Chen et al., 1993), we asked whether these sensors could be optimized to read out specific active DOR conformations at distinct subcellular locations.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Nb39 recognizes opioid receptor active conformations through residues conserved across MOR, KOR, and DOR.
source: We used the nanobody biosensor Nb39, which recognizes opioid receptor active conformations through residues conserved across MOR, KOR, and DOR (Che et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2015), and the miniGsi biosensor, which mimics the interaction of the Gαi protein with GPCRs (Wan et al., 2018; Nehmé et al., 2017), as two orthogonal readouts of DOR conformations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The miniGsi biosensor mimics the interaction of the Gαi protein with GPCRs.
source: We used the nanobody biosensor Nb39, which recognizes opioid receptor active conformations through residues conserved across MOR, KOR, and DOR (Che et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2015), and the miniGsi biosensor, which mimics the interaction of the Gαi protein with GPCRs (Wan et al., 2018; Nehmé et al., 2017), as two orthogonal readouts of DOR conformations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nb39 was rapidly recruited to PM DOR when cells were treated with SNC80.
source: When cells were treated with either small molecule agonist SNC80 or peptide DPDPE, Nb39 (Figure 1B–C) and miniGsi (Figure 1D–E) were rapidly recruited to DOR on the plasma membrane (PM DOR), as observed by a rapid increase in fluorescence.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Nb39 was rapidly recruited to PM DOR when cells were treated with DPDPE.
source: When cells were treated with either small molecule agonist SNC80 or peptide DPDPE, Nb39 (Figure 1B–C) and miniGsi (Figure 1D–E) were rapidly recruited to DOR on the plasma membrane (PM DOR), as observed by a rapid increase in fluorescence.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: miniGsi was rapidly recruited to PM DOR when cells were treated with SNC80.
source: When cells were treated with either small molecule agonist SNC80 or peptide DPDPE, Nb39 (Figure 1B–C) and miniGsi (Figure 1D–E) were rapidly recruited to DOR on the plasma membrane (PM DOR), as observed by a rapid increase in fluorescence.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: miniGsi was rapidly recruited to PM DOR when cells were treated with DPDPE.
source: When cells were treated with either small molecule agonist SNC80 or peptide DPDPE, Nb39 (Figure 1B–C) and miniGsi (Figure 1D–E) were rapidly recruited to DOR on the plasma membrane (PM DOR), as observed by a rapid increase in fluorescence.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Fluorescence of both Nb39 and miniGsi increased significantly after treatment with SNC80, but not inverse agonist ICI174864.
source: Fluorescence of both sensors increased significantly after treatment with either agonist, but not inverse agonist ICI174864 (ICI) (Figure 1F), indicating specificity of both sensors for an agonist-induced active conformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Fluorescence of both Nb39 and miniGsi increased significantly after treatment with DPDPE, but not inverse agonist ICI174864.
source: Fluorescence of both sensors increased significantly after treatment with either agonist, but not inverse agonist ICI174864 (ICI) (Figure 1F), indicating specificity of both sensors for an agonist-induced active conformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Recruitment of Nb39 and miniGsi to PM DOR was concentration-dependent and saturated at 10 μM SNC80.
source: Furthermore, recruitment of Nb39 and miniGsi to PM DOR was concentration-dependent and saturated at the concentration of SNC80 used in these experiments (10 μM) (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: miniGsi was more potently recruited to PM DOR than Nb39 in response to the agonist SNC80.
source: Concentration-response curves also revealed that miniGsi was more potently recruited to PM DOR than Nb39 in response to the agonist SNC80.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from concentration-response curves.

claim: DPDPE recruited Nb39 to PM DOR more strongly than SNC80.
source: Interestingly, DPDPE recruited Nb39 to PM DOR more strongly than SNC80 (Figure 1C,F), whereas the opposite trend was observed for miniGsi (Figure 1E–F), suggesting that these sensors might report selective conformations of DOR induced by different agonists.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1F.

claim: SNC80 recruited miniGsi to PM DOR more strongly than DPDPE.
source: Interestingly, DPDPE recruited Nb39 to PM DOR more strongly than SNC80 (Figure 1C,F), whereas the opposite trend was observed for miniGsi (Figure 1E–F), suggesting that these sensors might report selective conformations of DOR induced by different agonists.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and 1F.

claim: MiniGs was not recruited to PM DOR.
source: MiniGs, which mimics Gαs protein interaction with Gs-coupled GPCRs, was not recruited to PM DOR (Figure 1F), suggesting that the miniGsi sensor specifically reports activation of the Gi-coupled DOR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Newly synthesized DOR is retained in an intracellular compartment in neurons and PC12 cells acutely treated with nerve growth factor (NGF).
source: To test whether DOR localized to an intracellular compartment engages Nb39 or miniGsi differently upon activation by the same agonist, we took advantage of the fact that newly synthesized DOR is retained in an intracellular compartment in neurons and pheochromocytoma-12 cells (PC12 cells) (Figure 1H and I, yellow arrows) acutely treated with nerve growth factor (NGF) (Kim and von Zastrow, 2003; Shiwarski et al., 2017a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and experimental data shown in Figure 1H and 1I.

claim: Nb39 was rapidly recruited to intracellular SNAP-tagged DOR within 30 s when cells were treated with 10 µM SNC80.
source: When cells were treated with 10 µM SNC80, a membrane-permeable, small molecule agonist, Nb39 was rapidly recruited to intracellular SNAP-tagged DOR, within 30 s (Figure 1I, Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I and Video 1.

claim: Nb39 fluorescence in the region of the cell defined by IC DOR rapidly and significantly increased after SNC80 addition.
source: When quantitated, Nb39 fluorescence in the region of the cell defined by IC DOR rapidly and significantly increased after SNC80 addition (Figure 1K–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K-L.

claim: Nb39 recruitment to IC DOR was dynamic and required DOR activation, as the DOR antagonist naltrindole rapidly reversed this effect.
source: This Nb39 recruitment was dynamic and required DOR activation, as the DOR antagonist naltrindole rapidly reversed this effect (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: miniGsi was not recruited to IC DOR in the same time frame as Nb39.
source: In striking contrast to Nb39, miniGsi was not recruited to IC DOR in the same time frame (Figure 1J–K, Video 2), despite comparable levels of IC DOR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J-K and Video 2.

claim: MiniGsi fluorescence in the region of the cell defined by IC DOR did not increase in cells treated with SNC80.
source: MiniGsi fluorescence in the region of the cell defined by IC DOR did not increase in cells treated with SNC80 (Figure 1K–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K-L.

claim: miniGs was not recruited to IC DOR in cells treated with SNC80.
source: As a control, miniGs was also not recruited to IC DOR in cells treated with SNC80 (Figure 1L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Both Nb39 and miniGsi were recruited to PM DOR, as seen by confocal imaging in the same cells in which recruitment to IC DOR was measured.
source: Both sensors were recruited to PM DOR, as seen by confocal imaging in the same cells in which we measured recruitment to IC DOR, although the sensitivity of detection was lower in confocal imaging (Figure 1I–J, yellow arrowheads, and Figure 1M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I-J and 1M.

claim: MiniGsi was recruited to PM DOR more strongly than Nb39.
source: MiniGsi was recruited to PM DOR more strongly than Nb39 (Figure 1F,M), consistent with the TIR-FM results, which makes the absence of miniGsi recruitment to IC DOR in response to SNC80 even more striking.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and 1M.

claim: SNC80 promotes an active DOR conformation preferentially recognized by Nb39 in intracellular compartments and a distinct active DOR conformation preferentially recognized by miniGsi at the PM.
source: These results indicate that SNC80 promotes an active DOR conformation preferentially recognized by Nb39 in intracellular compartments and a distinct active DOR conformation preferentially recognized by miniGsi at the PM, suggesting location-specific conformational effects of SNC80 on DOR.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data presented.

claim: Nb39 was not recruited to IC DOR when cells were treated with 10 µM peptide agonist DPDPE.
source: When cells were treated with 10 µM peptide agonist DPDPE, which does not readily cross the PM over short time scales (Stoeber et al., 2018), Nb39 was not recruited to IC DOR (Figure 1L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: DPDPE does not readily cross the PM over short time scales.
source: When cells were treated with 10 µM peptide agonist DPDPE, which does not readily cross the PM over short time scales (Stoeber et al., 2018), Nb39 was not recruited to IC DOR (Figure 1L).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Activation of PM DOR is not sufficient for recruitment of Nb39 to IC DOR.
source: This suggests that activation of PM DOR is not sufficient for recruitment of Nb39 to IC DOR.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that DPDPE, which activates PM DOR but does not cross the membrane, does not recruit Nb39 to IC DOR.

claim: Nb39 was robustly recruited to IC DOR after 100 nM SNC80 addition, even when PM DOR was pharmacologically blocked with ICI.
source: Nb39 was robustly recruited to IC DOR, even when PM DOR was pharmacologically blocked, indicating that recruitment to IC DOR does not require activation of PM DOR (Figure 2A, top, 2B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, 2B, and 2C.

claim: Recruitment of Nb39 to IC DOR does not require activation of PM DOR.
source: Nb39 was robustly recruited to IC DOR, even when PM DOR was pharmacologically blocked, indicating that recruitment to IC DOR does not require activation of PM DOR (Figure 2A, top, 2B, C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Nb39 is recruited to IC DOR even when PM DOR is blocked.

claim: miniGsi remained diffuse throughout the cell and was not recruited to IC DOR when PM DOR was pharmacologically blocked.
source: When PM DOR was pharmacologically blocked, miniGsi again remained diffuse throughout the cell and was not recruited to IC DOR (Figure 2A, bottom, 2B, C), indicating that the absence of miniGsi recruitment to IC DOR is not due to sequestration of sensor at PM DOR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, 2B, and 2C.

claim: The absence of miniGsi recruitment to IC DOR is not due to sequestration of sensor at PM DOR.
source: When PM DOR was pharmacologically blocked, miniGsi again remained diffuse throughout the cell and was not recruited to IC DOR (Figure 2A, bottom, 2B, C), indicating that the absence of miniGsi recruitment to IC DOR is not due to sequestration of sensor at PM DOR.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that miniGsi is not recruited to IC DOR even when PM DOR is blocked.

claim: miniGsi was not recruited to IC DOR even in PTX-treated cells.
source: Even in PTX-treated cells, miniGsi was not recruited to IC DOR, suggesting that competition with endogenous Gαi/o protein effectors for interaction with DOR is not responsible for the lack of recruitment of miniGsi to IC DOR (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Competition with endogenous Gαi/o protein effectors for interaction with DOR is not responsible for the lack of recruitment of miniGsi to IC DOR.
source: Even in PTX-treated cells, miniGsi was not recruited to IC DOR, suggesting that competition with endogenous Gαi/o protein effectors for interaction with DOR is not responsible for the lack of recruitment of miniGsi to IC DOR (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that miniGsi is not recruited to IC DOR even when endogenous Gαi/o proteins are inactivated.

claim: Nb39 was recruited to IC DOR localized to the Golgi.
source: Immunofluorescence microscopy showed that Nb39 was recruited to IC DOR localized to the Golgi.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data.

claim: Only Nb39, and not miniGsi, was recruited to IC DOR in a region of the cell colocalizing with the TGN-38 marker in cells treated with CNA and SNC80.
source: Consistent with live-cell imaging data, only Nb39, and not miniGsi, was recruited to IC DOR in a region of the cell colocalizing with the TGN-38 marker (Figure 2D,E) in cells treated with CNA and SNC80.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: CNA alone did not cause recruitment of either Nb39 or miniGsi.
source: CNA alone did not cause recruitment of either sensor.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Treatment with CNA and SNC80 significantly increased Nb39 Golgi enrichment.
source: Treatment with CNA and SNC80 significantly increased Nb39 Golgi enrichment (Figure 2F), whereas miniGsi enrichment was not significantly different from control cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: miniGsi enrichment in the Golgi was not significantly different from control cells after treatment with CNA and SNC80.
source: Treatment with CNA and SNC80 significantly increased Nb39 Golgi enrichment (Figure 2F), whereas miniGsi enrichment was not significantly different from control cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Agonist-dependent differential biosensor recruitment to MOR and KOR in the PM correlates with recruitment of other receptor effectors, specifically G protein-coupled receptor kinase 2 (GRK2), which mediates receptor desensitization.
source: Agonist-dependent differential biosensor recruitment to MOR and KOR in the PM correlates with recruitment of other receptor effectors, specifically G protein-coupled receptor kinase 2 (GRK2), which mediates receptor desensitization (Stoeber et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: β-arrestins interact with DOR and other GPCRs after activation by agonists and receptor phosphorylation by GRKs to mediate receptor desensitization and internalization from the PM.
source: β-arrestins interact with DOR and other GPCRs after activation by agonists and receptor phosphorylation by GRKs to mediate receptor desensitization and internalization from the PM (Zhang et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 2005; Gurevich and Gurevich, 2019b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: β-arrestins can scaffold kinase-signaling complexes from GPCRs at the PM and endosomes.
source: β-arrestins can also scaffold kinase-signaling complexes from GPCRs at the PM and endosomes (Peterson and Luttrell, 2017; DeFea et al., 2000a; DeFea et al., 2000b; McDonald et al., 2000; Weinberg et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Neither β-arrestin-1 nor β-arrestin-2 was recruited to IC DOR in cells treated with SNC80.
source: Similar to miniGsi, neither β-arrestin-1 nor β-arrestin-2 was recruited to IC DOR in cells treated with SNC80, and no increase in fluorescence in the region of the cell defined by IC DOR was detected (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Both β-arrestin-1 and β-arrestin-2 were visibly recruited to the PM by confocal imaging in response to SNC80 treatment.
source: In contrast, both β-arrestins were visibly recruited to the PM by confocal imaging (Figure 3A,B, yellow arrowheads) and by quantitation of TIR-FM imaging (Figure 3D–F) in response to SNC80 treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, 3B, 3D, 3E, and 3F.

claim: β-arrestins interact with only agonist-activated DOR present in the PM.
source: Together, these data indicate that like miniGsi, β-arrestins interact with only agonist-activated DOR present in the PM.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that β-arrestins are recruited to PM DOR but not IC DOR.

claim: DOR couples primarily to Gαi/o proteins, which inhibit adenylyl cyclase activity to decrease cAMP.
source: Like the other opioid receptors, DOR couples primarily to Gαi/o proteins, which inhibit adenylyl cyclase activity to decrease cAMP (Gendron et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Addition of adenylyl cyclase activator forskolin (Fsk, 2 µM) caused a rapid increase in the cyan fluorescent protein (CFP/FRET) ratio over the baseline ratio in PC12 cells expressing ICUE3 and SNAP-DOR.
source: In PC12 cells expressing ICUE3 and SNAP-DOR, addition of adenylyl cyclase activator forskolin (Fsk, 2 µM) caused a rapid increase in the cyan fluorescent protein (CFP/FRET) ratio over the baseline ratio (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Pretreatment with 100 nM SNC80 prior to Fsk addition decreased the Fsk-stimulated cAMP response.
source: Pretreatment with 100 nM SNC80 prior to Fsk addition decreased the Fsk-stimulated cAMP response (Figure 4C–D), consistent with DOR activation inhibiting adenylyl cyclase activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: In cells with PM DOR only, SNC80 failed to decrease Fsk-stimulated cAMP in the presence of ICI.
source: In cells with PM DOR only, SNC80 failed to decrease Fsk-stimulated cAMP in the presence of ICI (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: In cells with IC DOR, SNC80 decreased Fsk-stimulated cAMP even in the presence of ICI.
source: In contrast, in cells with IC DOR, SNC80 decreased Fsk-stimulated cAMP even in the presence of ICI (Figure 4G–H), and significantly decreased endpoint and total cAMP levels (Figure 4I–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G-H and 4I-J.

claim: Golgi DOR activation is sufficient for cAMP inhibition.
source: These results indicate that Golgi DOR activation is sufficient for cAMP inhibition.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that IC DOR can inhibit cAMP even when PM DOR is blocked.

claim: IC DOR activation suppressed Fsk-stimulated cAMP to approximately half the degree suppressed by combined PM and IC DOR.
source: IC DOR activation suppressed Fsk-stimulated cAMP to approximately half the degree suppressed by combined PM and IC DOR (Figure 4I–J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I-J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ICI alone did not significantly affect endpoint or total cAMP levels.
source: As a control, ICI alone did not significantly affect endpoint or total cAMP levels (Figure 4I–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I-J.

claim: The permeable small molecule agonist SNC80 decreased Fsk-stimulated cAMP even in the presence of ICI in cells treated with LY294002.
source: Similar to results obtained in NGF-treated cells, the permeable small molecule agonist SNC80 decreased Fsk-stimulated cAMP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D) even in the presence of ICI, reiterating that Golgi DOR activation is sufficient for cAMP inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: The peptide DPDPE agonist did not decrease the Fsk response in the presence of ICI.
source: As a control, the peptide DPDPE agonist did not decrease the Fsk response in the presence of ICI (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, E, and F.

claim: DOR activation by the same agonist in different subcellular compartments promotes distinct active conformations recognized differentially by biosensors.
source: Together, our data suggest that DOR activation by the same agonist in different subcellular compartments promotes distinct active conformations recognized differentially by biosensors.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, inferred from the experimental results presented.

claim: The subcellular location in which receptors are activated might determine the conformational landscapes that receptors can adopt upon activation, because the immediate environment of receptors varies between these locations.
source: Our results suggest that the subcellular location in which receptors are activated might determine the conformational landscapes that receptors can adopt upon activation, because the immediate environment of receptors varies between these locations.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental results presented.

claim: Structures of MOR with agonist BU72 and KOR with agonist MP1104 share the outward shift of transmembrane helix (TM)6, which is characteristic of active GPCR structures.
source: Structures of MOR with agonist BU72 and KOR with agonist MP1104 share the outward shift of transmembrane helix (TM)6, which is characteristic of active GPCR structures (Che et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nb39 appears to stabilize the active conformation via contacts with intracellular loop (ICL)2 and ICL3, as well as the eighth helix through residues conserved across MOR, KOR, and DOR.
source: Nb39 appears to stabilize this conformation via contacts with intracellular loop (ICL)2 and ICL3, as well as the eighth helix through residues conserved across MOR, KOR, and DOR (Che et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The structure of MOR in complex with agonist DAMGO and the nucleotide-free Gαi protein is very similar to the MOR-Nb39 structure, with the exception of a greater displacement of TM6 toward TM7 and a decreased extension of ICL3.
source: The structure of MOR in complex with agonist [D-Ala2, N-MePhe4, Gly-ol5]-enkephalin (DAMGO) and the nucleotide-free Gαi protein is very similar to the MOR-Nb39 structure, with the exception of a greater displacement of TM6 toward TM7 and a decreased extension of ICL3 (Koehl et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: miniGs and Gαs contact B2AR similarly.
source: The miniGsi sensor does not contain all regions of Gαi that contact the receptor, but many of the residues that interact with MOR ICL2 and ICL3 via the Gαi C-terminal α5 helix are present in miniGsi, and previous reports show that miniGs and Gαs contact B2AR similarly (Nehmé et al., 2017; Carpenter et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Phospholipids differing in charge can stabilize active or inactive conformations of the β2-adrenergic receptor, stabilize G protein coupling, and modulate G protein selectivity.
source: Phospholipids differing in charge can stabilize active or inactive conformations of the β2-adrenergic receptor, stabilize G protein coupling, and modulate G protein selectivity (Dawaliby et al., 2016; Strohman et al., 2019; Yen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Lipid composition can influence recruitment of effectors like β-arrestins, which bind PI4,5P2, a phospholipid species enriched in the PM.
source: Lipid composition can also influence recruitment of effectors like β-arrestins, which bind PI4,5P2, a phospholipid species enriched in the PM (Gaidarov et al., 1999), potentially contributing to the lack of observed arrestin recruitment to Golgi DOR.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study and is used to speculate about the experimental results.

claim: β-arrestin recruitment to active GPCRs in the Golgi has not been reported.
source: To date, β-arrestin recruitment to active GPCRs in the Golgi has not been reported, and the impact of receptor localization to this compartment on desensitization, β-arrestin recruitment, and β-arrestin-biased signaling is not known.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The Golgi lumen is more acidic than the extracellular space, pH 6.4 vs pH 7.4.
